topic: Hotkey timestamp logger app for Streamlabs OBS (press key → log recording elapsed + wall-clock timestamp to a JSON file, simple desktop GUI)
initialPrompt: Im thinking of making an app that like I can press a keybind, and it like checks my streamlabs obs, and checks how long I've been recording, what the exact time stamp is, and then logs that timestamp down to a json file. Every time I press the hotkey, that timestamp gets logged. Is that possible? I would like it to be a simple desktop app with a gui. Ask me any questions if you have. This is just a brainstorm session, not a actual building session.

qAndA.question: SLOBS connectivity: use the official Streamlabs Remote API (JSON-RPC over SockJS WebSocket, token from Settings → Remote Control) as the primary source for recording state + elapsed time; fall back to SLOBS's bundled obs-websocket (rec-timecode) if unavailable. Implementation detail, no user-facing impact.

Session-aware logging: the app listens for recording start/stop events and tracks elapsed time locally, so a hotkey press reads the local clock + locally-tracked session start instead of an API round-trip; the API only confirms state and acts as fallback. More robust, near-zero latency.

Data file: a single JSON file (array of entries) next to the app, written atomically (temp file + rename) so a crash mid-write can't corrupt it. Matches the 'log to a json file' mental model and opens cleanly in any editor.

Entry schema: wall-clock ISO timestamp of the press + recording elapsed time (HH:MM:SS) + a session id so entries from different recording sessions are distinguishable; optional note field added later if the user wants it.
Not-recording presses: show a brief warning (toast/flash) and log nothing — pressing the hotkey while not recording is assumed to be a mistake.
Auto-log boundaries: recording started/stopped events are also written to the JSON (flagged as events, not presses) so the log is self-describing; pure hotkey-press log if the user vetoes.
App shape: Windows-first, tray-resident background app with a small always-on-top status window showing recording state, elapsed time, and last stamp; no installer, no accounts, no cloud.
Hotkey: configurable in the GUI with a sensible default (e.g., F8); rebinding is a GUI dropdown, not a config-file edit.

What will you actually DO with these logged timestamps? This changes the app's shape — e.g., if it's for marking moments to edit into highlights later, a 'quick note' feature and export-to-editor formats become valuable; if it's just 'proof of when I recorded', bare timestamps are enough. My recommendation: personal highlight marking for later video editing (the classic use for this exact workflow) — but tell me yours.

qAndA.question: App shape revision (user veto of #7): no always-on-top status window. The app lives in the tray; its main window is a log viewer listing recording sessions and their entries, where clicking an entry lets you type or edit a description. The full-log keybind opens a small description prompt.
Hotkey revision (user request): two configurable keybinds — quick log (no description required) and full log (opens a prompt requiring a description). Both rebindable in settings.
In-app log viewer (user requirement): view all logs grouped by recording session; click any entry to type or edit its description inside the app. Description is optional and editable after the fact.
Karpathy guidelines activated for this session: keep the design simple, make surgical scope choices, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria before building.
Entry id: each entry gets a stable auto-increment id so click-to-annotate and future editing/deletion can reference entries unambiguously.
Timestamp format: ISO 8601 wall-clock with timezone offset (human-readable in the raw JSON and unambiguous).

Elapsed time representation: store elapsed recording time as integer seconds (canonical, computable) and format to HH:MM:SS in the app UI; alternatively store the formatted string for raw-file readability. Which do you prefer?

qAndA.question: Delete/edit controls (user requirement): entries can be deleted (hard delete with a confirmation dialog — simplest, no tombstone complexity) and edited in the viewer (editing the description field; the timestamp and elapsed are treated as facts).

Session ↔ video file linkage: should each recording session in the log also record the output file SLOBS was writing (e.g., '2026-08-04 17-24-33.mp4'), so the app can later point you at — or even open — the exact clip for that session? This is high-value for your 'edit highlights later' workflow, and it's cheap if the API exposes the file path. Recommendation: yes — store the file name/path per session when available; opening the clip in a player is a phase-2 feature, not part of the core build.

Scene context per entry: should each log entry also record which SLOBS scene was active at the press (e.g., 'Game', 'BRB', 'Intro')? It would let you filter junk markers later, and it's one more event type to listen to. Recommendation: skip it for v1 — you didn't ask for it, it adds a second listener plus a field to maintain, and JSON is easy to extend later if you find yourself wanting it. Lean 'no' unless you have a concrete use in mind.

Distribution + stack: is this app just for you, or will other streamers use it? If just-for-you: Python 3 (pynput global hotkeys + websocket-client to SLOBS + tkinter GUI) — fastest to build and iterate, and a one-file JSON store next to the script. If it must ship to others: a single-exe build (C# WPF or a packaged PyInstaller app) so there's no runtime install. Recommendation: just-for-you, Python. If you have a language you'd rather write this in, say so now.
qAndA.answer: It will be made for myself and others aswell. I will give it to other devices.

qAndA.question: Stack decision (resolving distribution): Windows-only single-file .exe built with PyInstaller from the Python codebase — keeps the simple Python stack and its fast iteration while producing a distributable exe with no runtime install (caveat: SmartScreen/AV may warn on unsigned exes; C# WPF self-contained publish is the fallback if that becomes a problem). SLOBS is Windows-only, so Windows-only is assumed.

summary: Design for a Windows desktop app that logs Streamlabs OBS recording moments via hotkeys. Core: two rebindable global hotkeys — quick log (no description) and full log (description required via prompt). The app is session-aware: it listens to SLOBS recording start/stop events via the official Remote API (SockJS WebSocket + token; obs-websocket as fallback) and tracks elapsed time locally, so presses are near-instant. Data: single JSON array file written atomically next to the app; entries carry auto-increment id, ISO 8601 wall-clock timestamp with offset, elapsed seconds, description (null until filled), and press/event type; sessions group entries and carry a session id plus the SLOBS output file name when available; recording start/stop are auto-logged as events; presses while not recording show a warning and log nothing. UI: tray-resident app whose main window is a log viewer — sessions listed, click any entry to type or edit its description, delete with confirmation (hard delete); no always-on-top window. Distribution: ships to other streamers as a Windows-only single-file .exe via PyInstaller (SmartScreen caveat; C# WPF self-contained is the fallback). Deliberately out of scope for v1: scene context per entry, opening clips in a player, installer, cloud. Success criteria: quick-log press while recording appends an entry visible in the JSON and viewer within ~1s; full log without a description writes nothing; edits/deletes persist across restarts; the file stays valid under rapid presses.
